articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.3M tourism contract renewed without competitive bid
articles.dek: County commissioners quietly extended the agreement with a Tallahassee marketing firm last month. Public records show no other vendors were considered.
brief: Escambia County commissioners renewed a $2.3 million tourism marketing contract with Tallahassee-based Sachs Media in May without issuing a request for proposals
The three-year extension was approved on the consent agenda with no public discussion, according to meeting records
County purchasing policy allows no-bid renewals for professional services contracts, but some commissioners say the practice deserves more scrutiny
articles.body:
The contract extension appeared as item 14C on the May 21 consent agenda. No discussion. No questions from the dais. The vote took less than ten seconds.

That's how Escambia County renewed a $2.3 million agreement with Sachs Media Group, the Tallahassee firm that has managed the county's tourism marketing since 2020. The three-year extension runs through 2029.

Public records obtained by The Flightline show no evidence that county staff solicited proposals from other vendors before recommending renewal. No competitive analysis. No comparison pricing. The agenda packet contained the existing contract, a brief staff memo recommending extension, and nothing else.

How it happened

Escambia County's purchasing policy allows professional services contracts to be renewed without competitive bidding if the original agreement included renewal options. The 2020 Sachs contract did—two three-year extensions, exercisable at the county's discretion.

County Administrator Wes Moreno said the renewal followed proper procedure.

"This contract has performed well for the county," Moreno said in an email response to questions. "The vendor has met all deliverables, and renewal was the most efficient path forward."

The tourist development council, an advisory board that recommends how bed tax revenue is spent, reviewed the renewal at its April meeting. Minutes show the discussion lasted approximately four minutes. The board voted 6-1 to recommend approval.

Commissioner Mike Kohler, whose district includes Perdido Key, cast the lone dissenting vote on the TDC. He said he wanted to see what other firms might offer.

"Six years is a long time with one vendor," Kohler said. "I'm not saying they've done a bad job. I'm saying we don't know what we're missing."

What the contract covers

Sachs Media manages Visit Pensacola's advertising campaigns, media buys, social media presence, and public relations. The firm is paid through tourist development tax revenue—the 5% levy on short-term rentals that visitors pay, not general tax dollars.

Under the renewed contract, Sachs will receive approximately $767,000 annually. That's a 12% increase from the original 2020 agreement, which county officials attribute to expanded digital advertising requirements and inflation adjustments.

The firm's work has coincided with strong tourism numbers. Escambia County collected $21.4 million in bed tax revenue in fiscal year 2025, up from $14.8 million in 2020. But isolating the marketing firm's contribution from broader travel trends—including pandemic recovery and population growth in feeder markets like Birmingham and Atlanta—is difficult.

Sachs Media did not respond to a request for comment.

The policy question

No-bid contract renewals are common in Florida county government. State law gives local governments wide latitude in procurement, and many professional services agreements include multi-year renewal options to provide continuity.

But good-government advocates say the practice can insulate vendors from competition and make it harder to identify cost savings.

"Automatic renewals made sense when finding vendors was hard," said Ben Wilcox, research director at Integrity Florida, a nonpartisan ethics watchdog. "In the internet age, there's really no excuse not to at least test the market every few years."

Wilcox said his organization has tracked an increase in no-bid professional services contracts across Florida counties since 2018. He called Escambia's tourism contract "not unusual, but not best practice either."

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, who chairs the board, defended the renewal process. He said consent agenda items receive staff vetting before reaching commissioners.

"If there were problems with this vendor, we would have heard about it," Bergosh said. "I trust our tourism staff to flag concerns."

He acknowledged he had not personally reviewed alternative vendors before voting.

What's next

The renewed contract runs through May 2029. It contains one additional three-year renewal option, meaning Sachs could potentially hold the account through 2032—twelve consecutive years—without ever facing competitive bidding.

Kohler said he plans to propose a policy change requiring competitive solicitation for any professional services contract exceeding $500,000, regardless of renewal options. He does not yet have a co-sponsor.

"I'm not trying to create bureaucracy," he said. "I just think when you're spending this kind of money, you should know what else is out there."

The tourist development council's next meeting is scheduled for July 15.

articles.label: Development & Infrastructure
articles.headline: Six months after Ian settlement, Pensacola Beach rebuilding stalls over flood insurance gaps
articles.dek: Dozens of property owners say federal payouts covered less than half their damage. Some lots sit empty as summer season begins.
brief: At least 47 Pensacola Beach properties remain unrepaired or demolished six months after Hurricane Ian insurance settlements were finalized, according to Escambia County permit records.
Property owners interviewed by The Flightline say National Flood Insurance Program payouts averaged 40-60% of actual reconstruction costs, leaving gaps of $80,000 to $300,000.
Santa Rosa Island Authority officials warn that empty lots and half-finished structures could depress summer rental revenues by an estimated $2.3 million across the beach community.
articles.body:
The concrete slab at 1847 Via de Luna sits empty except for a rusted water heater and a child's bicycle frame. Eight months ago, this was a three-bedroom rental house that grossed $4,200 a week in peak season. Now it's a monument to what Cheryl Dawkins calls "the math that doesn't work."

"FEMA says the house was worth $340,000," Dawkins said, standing at the lot's edge on a Thursday morning. "They paid out $247,000. My contractor says $410,000 to rebuild to current code. So where does the other $163,000 come from?"

She's not alone. Across Pensacola Beach, at least 47 properties remain unrepaired, under-construction, or reduced to empty slabs six months after the National Flood Insurance Program finalized settlements for Hurricane Ian damage. The storm made landfall in late September 2025, its outer bands flooding the barrier island with four feet of surge in some areas.

The gap between federal payouts and actual rebuilding costs has frozen reconstruction on the island just as summer rental season begins.

The coverage gap

The National Flood Insurance Program caps residential payouts at $250,000 for structure damage. That limit hasn't changed since 1994, though construction costs in coastal Florida have more than doubled in that period.

"You're insuring a 2025 house with 1994 math," said Robert Kendall, a public adjuster who has handled 23 Pensacola Beach claims since Ian. "And that's before you get into the code upgrade requirements."

Florida building code changes enacted after Hurricane Michael in 2018 require substantially damaged structures—those with damage exceeding 50% of market value—to rebuild to current wind and flood standards. On Pensacola Beach, that often means elevating structures an additional three to five feet and installing impact-rated windows throughout.

Kendall estimates those code upgrades add $60,000 to $120,000 to typical rebuilding costs. NFIP policies include up to $30,000 for code compliance. The gap falls on property owners.

Escambia County property records show 89 Pensacola Beach structures were classified as substantially damaged after Ian. Of those, 42 have active rebuilding permits. The remaining 47 show no permit activity or have been reduced to cleared lots.

Rental revenue at risk

The Santa Rosa Island Authority, which manages leases for all private development on the beach, tracks rental properties through its lease compliance program. At a May meeting, Executive Director Paolo Ghio presented data showing 31 former rental units remain offline.

"These aren't second homes sitting empty," Ghio told the SRIA board. "These are revenue-generating properties. The owners are losing income. The county is losing bed tax. The businesses on the island are losing customers."

SRIA estimates those 31 offline units would have generated approximately $2.3 million in gross rental revenue during the June-August peak season. The county's 5% bed tax on that revenue—$115,000—funds beach maintenance and tourism marketing.

The authority has limited leverage. Lease agreements require properties to remain "in good repair," but Ghio said the SRIA has never terminated a lease over storm damage delays.

"These people aren't abandoning their properties," he said in an interview. "They're stuck. That's different."

Private insurance complications

Some property owners carry private flood insurance policies that exceed NFIP limits. But those policies have created their own complications.

Margaret and Dale Fontaine own a duplex on Ariola Drive that sustained $380,000 in damage. Their private flood policy through a surplus lines carrier covered up to $500,000. Seven months later, they've received $191,000.

"Every invoice we submit, they find something wrong with it," Dale Fontaine said. "Wrong date format. Contractor license expired by two weeks. Missing the third page of a four-page estimate. It's death by paperwork."

Their carrier, Palomar Specialty Insurance, declined to comment on specific claims. A spokesperson said the company "processes all claims according to policy terms and applicable regulations."

The Fontaines have hired an attorney. They're not alone in that either. Escambia County Circuit Court records show 14 flood insurance lawsuits filed since January involving Pensacola Beach properties. Three name NFIP's administrator, the Federal Emergency Management Agency. Eleven target private carriers.

The cost of waiting

Construction costs aren't static. The National Association of Home Builders tracks material and labor indices monthly. In the Pensacola metro area, both have risen since Ian.

Lumber costs are up 8% since October. Licensed contractor labor rates have increased 12%, driven partly by demand from Ian rebuilding across the Panhandle and lingering recovery work from earlier storms.

Every month a property owner waits, the gap between insurance payout and construction cost widens.

"I got my settlement in January," said Thomas Rourke, whose Via de Luna townhouse remains gutted to the studs. "Same contractor, same plans—the quote went up $34,000 between January and April. That money doesn't exist."

Rourke, a retired airline pilot, said he's considering selling the property as-is. Two investment groups have approached him with cash offers at roughly 60% of his pre-storm assessed value.

"I didn't want to be a landlord anyway," he said. "My wife and I bought this place to retire here. That dream's gone. Now I just want out without going bankrupt."

Limited options

Property owners facing coverage gaps have few good options. FEMA's Increased Cost of Compliance coverage maxes out at $30,000. Small Business Administration disaster loans require repayment with interest. Home equity lines require equity that storm damage often erases.

Florida's My Safe Florida Home program offers grants up to $10,000 for wind hardening but doesn't cover flood-related construction. The state's hurricane relief fund, depleted by prior storms, has no active disbursement program for individual property owners.

State Rep. Alex Andrade, R-Pensacola, said he plans to file legislation in the 2027 session addressing the gap between NFIP limits and actual construction costs. But that's 18 months away and would require federal coordination.

"This is fundamentally a federal program failing to keep pace with reality," Andrade said. "The state can do some things around the margins. But the core problem is a $250,000 cap set 30 years ago."

Summer arrives

Memorial Day weekend brought the usual surge of visitors to Pensacola Beach. The main commercial district along Fort Pickens Road hummed with families. Casino Beach filled early.

But east of Portofino, the damage remains visible. Blue tarps still cover three roofs on Panferio Drive. A two-story house on Avenida 18 stands windowless, its interior open to the elements. Hand-painted signs reading "PRIVATE PROPERTY NO TRESPASSING" mark several empty lots.

Cheryl Dawkins visits her empty slab most weeks. She files paperwork, talks to contractors, runs the numbers again.

"I'm 58 years old," she said. "I don't have another 30-year mortgage in me. But I can't sell this lot for what I owe on it. So I just come out here and stare at it and try to figure something out."

She doesn't have a solution yet. Neither, it seems, does anyone else.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's newest Blue Angels pilots train for their first hometown show
articles.dek: Two first-year demonstration pilots prepare for the July airshow at their home station, where 100,000 spectators will watch them fly.
brief: Lt. Cmdr. Marcus Webb and Lt. Amanda Chen are preparing for their first Pensacola Beach Airshow as Blue Angels demonstration pilots
The July 10-11 show at NAS Pensacola typically draws 100,000 spectators to the team's home station
Both pilots completed training at the squadron's El Centro winter facility and have flown 23 shows this season
articles.body:
The six F/A-18 Super Hornets banked hard over Pensacola Bay at 400 miles per hour Tuesday morning, their white contrails dissolving into the Gulf humidity. From the observation deck at Sherman Field, the roar arrived two seconds after the jets passed—a rolling thunder that rattled the metal bleachers and silenced the mockingbirds in the live oaks.

For Lt. Cmdr. Marcus Webb, flying the No. 3 right wing position, and Lt. Amanda Chen in the No. 4 slot, this practice run carried weight the crowds won't see. In five weeks, they'll perform at the Pensacola Beach Airshow in front of 100,000 spectators. It will be their first hometown show as Blue Angels pilots.

"Every show matters," Webb said after climbing down from his cockpit, flight suit dark with sweat. "But this one's different. My kids are going to be on that beach. My neighbors. The people I see at the grocery store."

The long road to the diamond

Webb and Chen joined the Blue Angels last September, selected from a pool of 30 applicants to fill two of the team's six demonstration pilot slots. Both are combat veterans—Webb flew missions over Syria and Iraq, Chen deployed twice to the Western Pacific. Both graduated from the Navy's elite TOPGUN school at NAS Fallon in Nevada.

None of that fully prepared them for formation flying at 18 inches of separation.

"In the fleet, if you're within a wingspan of another aircraft, something has gone very wrong," Chen said. "Here, we're so close I can see the rivets on Marcus's jet."

The team spent January through March at Naval Air Facility El Centro in California's Imperial Valley, where clear skies and sparse population allow intensive training away from the operational tempo of their home station. Webb and Chen flew twice daily, building muscle memory for the 35 maneuvers in the team's demonstration sequence.

By the time they arrived back at Forrest Sherman Field in late March, they had logged more than 120 training flights. Since then, they've performed at 23 shows across the country, from Lakeland, Florida, to Duluth, Minnesota.

Precision measured in inches

The Blue Angels' signature diamond formation requires four pilots to maintain their positions within 18 inches of the aircraft ahead and beside them. At demonstration speeds, a one-second lapse in concentration covers 600 feet of sky.

Capt. Brian Kesselring, the team's commanding officer and flight leader, sets the pace. He doesn't use radio calls during maneuvers—the other pilots watch his aircraft and react to its movements. It's called "Boss is always right" flying, and it demands absolute trust.

"When Boss moves, we move," Webb said. "There's no thinking. There's no deciding. Your body just follows."

The team practices at NAS Pensacola every Tuesday and Wednesday when not on the road. These sessions draw small crowds of aviation enthusiasts to the public viewing area along Radford Boulevard, but the real audience comes in July.

A hometown tradition

The Pensacola Beach Airshow has anchored the city's summer calendar since 1998. The Blue Angels have headlined every year except 2013, when sequestration grounded military demonstration teams, and 2020, when the pandemic canceled the event.

This year's show runs July 10-11. The team will perform their full demonstration both days, weather permitting, with the Friday show typically drawing a smaller but more aviation-focused crowd. Saturday brings the masses—families staking out spots on Casino Beach by sunrise, coolers and canopies spread across the sand.

For the first-year pilots, the hometown show adds a layer of pressure that distant venues don't.

"At other shows, if you have a rough day, you fly home and nobody knows," Chen said. "Here, everyone knows. Your neighbors saw it. The guy who changes your oil saw it. There's nowhere to hide."

She paused. "But that's also what makes it special. These are our people."

The view from the ground

The Blue Angels' presence shapes Pensacola in ways beyond the annual airshow. The team employs 140 enlisted sailors and officers at their Forrest Sherman Field headquarters. Their C-130 transport aircraft, nicknamed "Fat Albert," is a common sight over the city when moving equipment for road shows.

And twice a week during the season, the jets remind residents they live in a Navy town.

At Shoreline Park South in Gulf Breeze, a dozen regulars gather every Tuesday morning with folding chairs and binoculars. They track the aircraft by sound first, then spot them as silver glints against the clouds.

"Been coming out here 15 years," said retired machinist Mike Thornton, 71, who wore a faded Blue Angels cap from the 2009 season. "Never gets old. Never will."

Webb and Chen are aware of these informal audiences. The team's public affairs office tracks social media posts from the practice-day faithful, and the pilots occasionally wave from the observation deck before walking to their jets.

"Those folks are part of the family," Webb said. "They're out there in January when it's 40 degrees. They're out there in August when it's 95. They don't have to do that. They choose to."

What comes next

The Blue Angels will perform at shows in Traverse City, Michigan, and Dayton, Ohio, before returning for the Pensacola Beach event. After the hometown show, the schedule runs through November, ending with the traditional homecoming show at NAS Pensacola.

For Webb and Chen, this first season is about building consistency. They'll serve on the team for two years before rotating back to the fleet, replaced by the next class of applicants willing to trade combat flying for precision choreography.

"Two years sounds like a long time," Chen said. "But the shows come fast. The season's half over and it feels like we just got here."

Above the bay, the jets regrouped for another pass. Six aircraft, 18 inches apart, moving like a single organism. The sound rolled across the water, and the mockingbirds stayed silent a little longer.
